title: Thin skin
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative; your institution’s emergency pathway and the treating team’s judgment come first.
intro: You are the access surgeon in clinic. Mrs. Rosario Dela Paz, 63, has had a left upper-arm fistula for nine years. Most cannulations have used one segment, which is now a 3.5 cm aneurysm. Over its top the skin is thin and shiny with a small ulcer. Her venous pressures have been rising for two months. She has not bled. Her next dialysis is tomorrow morning, and she would like to keep using “the easy spot.”

choices.text: No cannulation of the threatened skin. Book prompt surgical repair, and image the outflow, because rising venous pressures suggest a stenosis raising the pressure in the aneurysm.
choices.feedback: Thin, shiny skin with an ulcer means the barrier has almost gone. Never needle threatened skin. An outflow stenosis raises the pressure and must be treated with the aneurysm.

choices.text: She has not bled, so the usual site can be used; review in three months.
choices.feedback: Ulcerated skin over an aneurysm signals impending rupture. A needle there could start a bleed she might not survive, and most fatal access bleeds happen at home.
choices.then: You change the plan: no cannulation of that skin, prompt repair, outflow imaging.

choices.text: Ask the unit to send monthly photographs so you can watch it.
choices.feedback: A photograph cannot establish that skin is safe. Thin, ulcerated skin needs action, not surveillance.
choices.then: You book prompt repair and outflow imaging, and tell the unit not to cannulate that skin.

choices.text: Agree a safe plan with the nephrologist and the unit: cannulate a healthy segment well away from the threatened skin if one exists; otherwise a temporary catheter.
choices.feedback: The access plan and the dialysis plan go together. If no safe segment exists, a temporary catheter until the repair is safer than needling threatened skin.

vitals.dialysis: Proximal healthy segment; catheter if needed

choices.text: Leave it to the unit to find a site.
choices.feedback: The nurses need a clear instruction from you and the nephrologist: which segment, and what to avoid.
choices.then: You call the unit and the nephrologist with a specific plan.

vitals.dialysis: Proximal healthy segment; catheter if needed

choices.feedback: Missed dialysis carries its own risks, such as high potassium and fluid overload. Find a safe route instead.
choices.then: You agree a safe segment with the nephrologist.

vitals.dialysis: Proximal healthy segment; catheter if needed

n3.scene: Before the repair date, the emergency department calls at 02:10. She woke bleeding from the aneurysm; her husband pressed a towel on it and brought her in. A nurse is applying a thick pressure dressing, and the emergency physician wants CT angiography “to see the anatomy.”

choices.text: Replace the bulky dressing with firm, focused pressure on the bleeding point with one or two fingers; lay her flat; resuscitate per protocol; no imaging while it bleeds; I am coming to control it.
choices.feedback: Focused pressure on the point stops access bleeding; a large dressing spreads the pressure. Imaging, photographs, and paperwork come after control.

choices.text: Get the CT angiogram first so I can plan the repair.
choices.feedback: Sending a bleeding patient to the scanner loses minutes she may not have. Control the bleeding first.
choices.then: You cancel the scan and ask for focused two-finger pressure until you arrive.

choices.text: The pressure dressing is fine; observe her until morning.
choices.feedback: A bulky dressing can look controlled while bleeding continues underneath. Thin skin that has bled once will bleed again.
choices.then: The dressing soaks through. You ask for focused pressure and come in.

choices.text: Control and repair the aneurysm, treat the outflow stenosis that raised the pressure, and arrange the next dialysis route with the nephrologist in case the access is lost.
choices.feedback: The UKKA 2025 guideline suggests surgical repair as the main approach, combined with treatment of downstream stenosis where appropriate. The access may be lost, so a dialysis plan is part of the operation.

vitals.dialysis: Repaired; outflow treated; catheter backup planned

choices.text: Ligate the fistula and let the nephrologist sort out dialysis later.
choices.feedback: Ligation may sometimes be needed, but ending her access without a plan leaves her without dialysis. Consider repair, and plan the next route now.

vitals.dialysis: Repaired; outflow treated; catheter backup planned

choices.feedback: Repair without treating the outflow stenosis leaves the high pressure that drove the aneurysm, and it may recur.

vitals.dialysis: Repaired; outflow treated; catheter backup planned

n5.prompt: What do she and her husband need to know?

choices.text: Teach both of them: press firmly with two fingers on the bleeding spot, keep pressing, call emergency help, and do not lift to look; give them the unit’s and your numbers and the nearest hospital that can treat a bleed.
choices.feedback: Most fatal access bleeds happen at home. Every patient and household member should know the response, taught and repeated, especially once an aneurysm appears.

choices.text: “If it bleeds, put a towel on it and come to the hospital.”
choices.feedback: A towel spreads the pressure. Two fingers on the spot, kept there, while help is called.

choices.text: Give them a leaflet on access care.
choices.feedback: A leaflet helps, but the response must be shown and practiced so it is automatic.

end.title: Day 3
end.text: The repaired fistula has a good thrill, and she dialyzes through a healthy segment. Her husband demonstrates two-finger pressure on the ward. The unit adds a bleeding drill to its monthly emergency practice and reviews its cannulation rotation.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Never needle threatened skin. Thin, shiny, ulcerated, or scabbed skin means impending rupture.
  • Look for the outflow stenosis behind a growing aneurysm.
  • Major bleed: focused two-finger pressure, lie flat, resuscitate, transfer. No imaging while it bleeds.
  • Repair and treat the outflow; plan the next dialysis route.
  • Teach the household; most fatal bleeds happen at home.

See Why access bleeding can be fatal, Responding to a major bleed and Teaching.
